newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judges accuse Chirac of interference.
newsitem.headline: French judges accuse Chirac of interference.

text.p: Senior French judges have accused President Jacques Chirac of interfering with the independence of the justice system by insisting on the appointment of key law officials against the advice of an independent watchdog.

The annual report by the Higher Magistrates' Council (CSM), published by the left-wing daily Liberation on Wednesday a day before it is to be presented to Chirac, complained that the president had overruled it in almost half the cases in which it had opposed particular appointments.
The report boosted opposition charges that the ruling Gaullist RPR party is packing the judiciary to block embarrassing corruption probes.
The investigations involve alleged illicit funding of the party via kickbacks on public housing contracts while Chirac was mayor of Paris in 1977-95.

Justice Minister Jacques Toubon told reporters after a weekly cabinet meeting he had not yet read the report but called the criticism "a storm in a teacup" and deplored what he called "political exploitation of justice matters".
The CSM complained that its recommendations against certain appointments had been overridden in 46 percent of cases in 1996. "This is a break with past practice," it was quoted as saying.
Government intervention in nominations "fuels suspicion among judges and the public about the independence of the magistrates concerned from political authorities," it said.
Liberation said Toubon had tried to suppress the report, an embarrassment for Chirac, who called in January for reforms to guaranteee the independence of the justice system.

But the minister said: "The truth is simple. Since July 1995, there have been almost 500 appointments of prosecutors. In seven cases, that is to say 1.5 percent, the government appointed magistrates against the opinion of the CSM, as the constitution allows."
The report recommended the justice minister be stripped of the power to order sensitive investigations pursued or shelved.
Liberation quoted a CSM member as saying that the ministry had sought to block publication of the report.

"No budget was allocated to the Council, there was a threat that it would be given no money to print the report...The authorities cannot accept these proposals which imply a strengthening of the CSM's powers," the unnamed member said.
Last July, the government filled the jobs of prosecutor at the Paris Appeals Court and the Supreme Court with Alexandre Benmakhlouf and Jean-Francois Burgelin, former aides to Chirac and Toubon.
In August, the government appointed a magistrate close to the Gaullist party as director of criminal affairs and pardons, a highly sensitive Justice Ministry position.

Benmakhlouf has under his control all the magistrates investigating alleged kickbacks at the Paris housing authority to feed Gaullist slush funds, the allocation of low-rent city-owned housing to relatives and political cronies and several other scandals involving the ruling parties.
Chirac appointed a panel of experts in January to propose reforms to better guarantee the independence of the justice system and protect the presumption of innocence.

The president sounded a note of caution on the central issue of cutting the umbilical cord between prosecutors and the justice ministry, saying the full implications of such a move needed to be examined thoroughly.
